title: Falcons training camp takeaways: Checking on quarterback, the offensive line and more Ahead of the Falcons' first preseason game of the season Friday against the Broncos, we look at what's been going on in camp. Josh Kendall

full_text:
Tua Tagovailoa is on track to be the Week 1 starter, but his injury history is worrisome. Dale Zanine / Imagn Images
The Atlanta Falcons are about two weeks into training camp, and that seemed like a good time for me to share my most pertinent thoughts. Let’s dive in.
I tried to come up with a sunnier way to say this, but quarterback is a mess at the moment. Tua Tagovailoa is coming off one of his worst professional seasons and was limited for the first seven practices by back tightness he began experiencing for the first time in his career shortly before training camp. You can’t question Tagovailoa’s toughness. In his career, he has had a high ankle sprain that required surgery, a hip dislocation that also required surgery and multiple concussions. He’s the strong favorite to start Week 1 at this point, but his injury history is not comforting.
Michael Penix Jr. (left ACL) still hasn’t been cleared for 11-on-11 work in practice, and he told reporters Wednesday he did not have a follow-up appointment scheduled with the surgeon who will sign off on his full participation. Penix, who has a tattered injury history of his own, is improving but trying to remain patient, he said.
“I’m running my own race,” he said. “I just have to take it one day at a time and focus on what I can control. Right now I can’t control not being out there.”
Meanwhile, training camp addition Cooper Rush seems to be slowly nudging out Jack Strand in the rotation, which was expected considering Rush is an eight-year NFL veteran. Rush and Strand split reps with the second team in 11-on-11 work during Saturday night’s practice at Lanier High School.
Overall, the quarterbacks’ results on the practice field are as smooth as you would expect, considering the jumbled rotation, intermittent availability and four quarterbacks learning a new offense. Saturday night, at least, provided some optimism as Tagovailoa was sharp and had nice throws for big gains to Olamide Zaccheaus and Drake London.
The Kansas City Chiefs may be about to start an undrafted rookie free agent, Kahlil Benson, at right tackle. Why does that matter for the Falcons? Because both of Kansas City’s right tackles from the last two years are in Atlanta. The Chiefs allowed Jawaan Taylor to leave via free agency and then traded Wanya Morris to the Falcons in June for a late-round pick swap. That Kansas City didn’t want to hold on to either player is not comforting, given its current state at the position.
The worst part is neither guy is playing right tackle for Atlanta right now. Taylor has not practiced with the team since signing because he is recovering from elbow and triceps injuries suffered last season. Head coach Kevin Stefanski said Taylor is attending all the team’s walkthroughs and meetings and is “close” to returning. Morris, who has missed several days due to a lower-body injury, has worked mostly at left tackle so far, although Stefanski said he will train on both sides.
So who are the Falcons’ right tackles right now? Michael Jerrell, a third-year sixth-round pick with three NFL starts; Brandon Walton, a fourth-year former undrafted free agent with two NFL starts; and Ethan Onianwa, the Falcons’ seventh-round pick this year.
General manager Ian Cunningham and his staff are almost certainly scouting the other 31 training camps for right tackles who might get cut when rosters are trimmed to 53 later this month.
There might be hope we won’t have to watch one of the worst screen games in the NFL this year, so that’ll be nice. Under Stefanski and offensive line coach Bill Callahan, the Falcons seem committed to improving. They are at least putting in the time at practice.
Atlanta is dedicating 10-minute chunks of practice to screens during some practices, left tackle Jake Matthews said.
“Callahan always says, ‘Every screen is different.’ You are never going to get two of the same. It’s really important to practice every type of look you can get,” he said. “You can run the exact same look, and it can play out three different ways.”
The Falcons ranked 26th in the league in EPA per pass play on screens (minus-.25) the last two years, according to TruMedia. It’s not that they didn’t try them. They were 13th in that span with 80 screen completions. They just didn’t work. Atlanta got only 5.8 percent of its passing yards from screens, a mark that ranked 29th in the league.
“The more you get confidence with the guys next to you, those plays can pop and they can be really, really explosive,” Matthews said.
With Bijan Robinson and Zachariah Branch, the Falcons seem well suited to heavy use of screens.
I’m worried many Falcons fans aren’t prepared for the length of suspension James Pearce Jr. is going to get. I would expect the league to announce his punishment under the personal conduct policy before rosters are trimmed at the end of this month. It’s going to be at least eight games, in my opinion. Based on the league’s previous rulings in similar situations and the details of Pearce’s February arrest and subsequent three felony charges , I wouldn’t be shocked if it was more.
Atlanta doesn’t appear to be planning on having Pearce early in the season. He has worked mostly with the third team so far, although Saturday night he took some snaps with the first and second units.
I’m good with Cunningham being aggressive on new contracts to lock up the team’s young offensive players. The Robinson and London deals were no-brainers. The Kyle Pitts and Matthew Bergeron contracts can be debated, but Cunningham looks like he got ahead of the market (or at least not behind it) on both deals.
One day after the Falcons made Pitts the third-highest-paid tight end in the league ($18 million), the Jaguars paid Brenton Strange $12 million a year. Strange has 986 receiving yards in three seasons. Less than a week after Atlanta made Bergeron the highest-paid guard in the league ($24 million per year), the Titans topped it with Peter Skoronski’s deal ($25 million per year), continuing a trend of skyrocketing salaries for the position in the last year.
If Pitts and Bergeron don’t perform at the level expected of players making that kind of money, Cunningham will get dinged for it. Right now, these are sensible deals.
The London, Robinson and Pitts contracts have a combined 15 void years tacked on the end, according to OverTheCap.com. The full details of the Bergeron deal aren’t available yet, but it’s likely similar. Void years are essentially extra seasons added to the end of contracts, allowing the salary cap hit to be spread out. Bryce Johnston, Atlanta’s senior vice president of football administration (cap guy), came from Philadelphia, which has used void years liberally to build its roster.
Those void years are one reason Atlanta is projected to have the second-most available salary cap space in the league in 2027 even after all the new deals.
Christian Harris is not quite a lock to start at middle linebacker. Rookies Kendal Daniels and Harold Perkins Jr. each got more time with the starters in practice last week. That may be the coaching staff getting a good look at them before they have to start making depth chart decisions, but it could mean more.
Harris, a third-round pick of the Texans in 2022 who has 27 career starts, is still the favorite to start Week 1 simply because of experience, but it’s good news for Atlanta that the young guys are coming along.
The live tackling at Falcons practices is new, and probably a preview of a change in the preseason plan. Atlanta did not have any live tackling in its training camp practices under previous head coaches Arthur Smith and Raheem Morris, but Stefanski has a different philosophy.
“I think there is a way to work hard and work smart and practice live because that’s what the game is,” he said. “I think there’s a way to do it safely. I think the guys understand how to do that the right way. You’re still not taking a shot on one of your teammates, but like I’ve said before, to get ready to…

full_text:
The Ravens drafted Ja'Kobi Lane in the third round and now the rookie receiver looks like he's in the running for the No. 3 receiver role. Mitch Stringer / Imagn Images
OWINGS MILLS, Md. — The Baltimore Ravens have spent weeks building toward the preseason. Saturday night, they finally get to see what they have.
Player evaluations feel premature until padded practices begin. Once they do, the next phase of the evaluation process comes when the games start. Coaches and team officials want to see how players — particularly the young ones — react when the lights go on.
The Ravens have had 10 practices in training camp, enough of a sample to get a good idea of where guys currently stand. However, the real tests will come this week and next, starting with Saturday night’s preseason opener. The following week, the Ravens have two joint practices against the Minnesota Vikings and then preseason game No. 2 on Aug. 22.
Until then, let’s examine the stock rosters and fallers through nearly two weeks of training camp.
His daily acrobatic catches and chunk plays have been the talk of training camp and silenced, at least for now, the talk that the Ravens need to go out and add a veteran receiver to join Zay Flowers and Rashod Bateman. A rookie third-round pick, Lane’s roster spot was secure. However, it’s looking more and more like he’s going to be on the field a lot for the Ravens when the regular season begins. He’s authoring one of the more impressive training camps for a Ravens rookie in recent memory.
Martin defied the odds to make the 53-man roster last year as an undrafted free agent. He’s well on his way to doing it again as long as the issue that kept him out of Baltimore’s last practice isn’t anything significant. His sticky coverage and penchant for being around the ball has made the slot corner an early practice standout. The Ravens probably have five cornerback locks in Marlon Humphrey, Nate Wiggins, Chidobe Awuzie, T.J. Tampa and fifth-round rookie Chandler Rivers. If they take a sixth, Martin seemingly has the lead over a host of young corners.
When the Ravens signed veteran Ethan Pocic about a week before training camp, the sense was that Pinter’s days working with the starting unit were numbered. That hasn’t been the case. Pinter continues to get almost all of the first-team starting center reps as Pocic works his way back from an Achilles injury and learns the offense. Meanwhile, coach Jesse Minter continues to say he views this as a legitimate competition at center. Pinter, without a doubt, is getting the longest audition, and the 30-year-old, who has made 10 career starts, has played well.
Robinson was always going to have a notable role on this team as an early down edge setter who beats up on running backs and tight ends. Robinson, however, has clearly added to his pass-rushing repertoire and has given Ravens tackles headaches throughout training camp. Whether it’s on the edge or inside, Robinson seems intent on making it awfully hard for the coaching staff to take him off the field. He could become the latest defensive Raven to break out in a contract year.
The Ravens have gotten trade calls on Tampa over the past 10 months, but they are reluctant to move him, because they view the 2024 fourth-round pick as a capable starter. Tampa hasn’t gotten that opportunity yet, but if he keeps playing like this, Minter will almost certainly find ways to get him on the field defensively. Tampa just hasn’t given up many plays in camp and he’s stood out both in one-on-one and team options. He could be pushing the veteran Awuzie for that No. 3 outside cornerback role.
The second-year offensive tackle has been far from flawless. He’s had some poor reps, but his overall consistency has improved significantly. He’s looked like one of the Ravens’ most improved players from last year. He’s cleaned up his technique and played with physicality and intensity, starring in several of the one-on-one periods against edge rushers. He appears well on his way to locking down the swing tackle role.
Honorable mention: Dominic DeLuca, ILB; Keondre Jackson, S; Tyler Loop, K; Amani Oruwariye, CB; Adam Randall, RB
Minter has repeatedly included Bullock in the starting center mix when asked, but to no fault of the former Terp, he’s probably out of time. He missed time early in camp while on the non-football illness list. He’s since returned, but he’s mostly just doing individual work and not participating in team sessions. His focus probably has to shift to making the team as a reserve interior lineman, and that could be an uphill battle.
Peebles probably hasn’t lost any traction in his bid to secure one of the reserve defensive line spots. Yet with so many of the veteran defensive linemen still working their way back to practice, there was an opening for Peebles to get a ton of front-line reps. Instead, Peebles went down with an undisclosed injury and missed most of practice last week. If Nnamdi Madubuike, Calais Campbell, Travis Jones, Broderick Washington Jr. and John Jenkins are all healthy, they are probably roster locks, and that leaves maybe one other spot for Peebles, C.J. Okoye and rookie Rayshaun Benny.
Wade was a longshot to make the 53-man roster from the start. However, he had a shot to at least force the team’s decision-makers to make a tough call if he was able to continue his strong form from the offseason practices. He has not been able to do that and has missed about a week now with an undisclosed injury. Health issues have slowed Wade the past two years, and he’s dealing with them again at the most inopportune time.
The 2024 fourth-round pick has made his share of plays in camp. He looks far more comfortable and assertive than he did last summer, and he’s also managed to avoid the nagging injuries that have dogged him through his first two years. Still, the sense coming into camp was that he was the favorite to be the team’s No. 3 wide receiver. Lane clearly appears to be that guy now, and fellow rookie Elijah Sarratt figures to challenge Walker for snaps as well.
Signed late in the offseason, Wallace has had a solid camp and done nothing with his play to get on this part of the list. Still, circumstances out of his control could create a roster squeeze that could impact the Ravens’ ability to keep Wallace as the fifth safety. One, core special teamer Keondre Jackson is having a strong training camp, and the coaching staff could be gaining more and more confidence in him as the No. 4 safety. And two, there are so many corners playing well. That could create a situation where the Ravens keep an extra corner at the expense of a fifth safety.

full_text:
Bryce Young is entering his fourth season with the Panthers, and coaches and teammates have noticed a difference in the QB this training camp. Jim Dedmon / Imagn Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — Carolina Panthers quarterbacks have made a lot of headlines in recent days, and none of them involved Bryce Young.
Kenny Pickett started the first preseason game and led a touchdown drive on his third series. Haynes King took over for Pickett, took over the game and then went from Hall of Fame Game hero to the injured list .
Former Florida and Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Kyle Trask was signed in the wake of King’s hamstring injury and showed up Sunday wearing Andy Dalton’s old No. 14 jersey.
Meanwhile, Young was relegated to a new space — in the background. The 2021 Heisman Trophy winner and the No. 1 pick in the 2023 NFL Draft led the Panthers’ offense through a half-speed, pregame practice in Canton, Ohio, then walked off Tom Benson Hall of Fame Stadium wearing a big smile after King’s game-winning touchdown.
Young and his teammates were back on the practice fields Sunday morning, when Young resumed what has been an exceptional training camp. He has fired darts to Tetairoa McMillan in the back of the end zone, feathered a touch pass to a well-covered Ja’Tavion Sanders along the sideline and slipped out of the pocket and found receivers on off-platform plays.
It’s too bad fans haven’t been able to see it.
Now in his third year in the Dave Canales/Brad Idzik offense, Young has the look of a composed quarterback who knows where the ball is supposed to go and knows he’s going to get it there.
“Just being here for the last year and a half, I’d say he just seems more comfortable,” said Mitchell Evans, the second-year tight end. “Even from when I first got here to now, he seems more confident in himself. And just the way he carries himself, he’s got more of a presence. And you can see that reflected on the field and even in the locker room and throughout the building. You can see he’s more confident.”
Young has come a long way since his five-game benching in 2024 during Canales’ first season in Charlotte. He’s improved each of the past two seasons, though he’s still a ways away from being considered among the league’s top quarterbacks.
In The Athletic ’s Mike Sando’s annual quarterback rankings — based on polling of 50 executives and coaches — Young landed in the third of four tiers and ranked 22nd among 35 QBs. That was a slight improvement from 2025 when Young ranked 24th.
Like Evans, at least one coach polled by Sando saw a more confident quarterback.
“His command, his confidence, his accuracy, the movement — he just seemed so much more confident as a player,” said the coach, whose team played the Panthers in the second half of the 2025 season. “It was an eye-opener for all of us to watch him perform. It reflected in their team.”
The Panthers view Young as an ascending player but aren’t ready to pay him quite yet. The team plans to let Young play out this season before deciding on a second contract.
Inconsistency has helped hold Young back. But with a solid cast of playmakers around him, led by McMillan, the 2025 Offensive Rookie of the Year, maybe this is the year Young makes a big leap in his development.
“I try to feed off the people around me. All of us are pushing each other, wanting to be at our best,” Young said Sunday. “Coaching staff challenging me, challenging all of us to take that next step system-wise. It’s just about having that growth mindset.
“For me, I just try to be where my feet are, make sure I’m focused. Whatever happens in the future, happens in the future. When you start thinking about that, you’re not able to focus on where you’re at.”
Where Young will be this weekend is Buffalo, where he’ll help break in the Bills’ new $2.1 billion stadium. Young will be more of an active participant than he was in Canton: Canales said he plans to play Young and the other starters between 10 and 20 reps, depending on how the offensive possessions play out.
If Young’s rep count turns out to be on the high side, he could eclipse his playing time for all of last preseason. Young played two series in the first two exhibitions (totaling 20 snaps) before sitting out the final tune-up against the Pittsburgh Steelers.
“I’m excited just to be able to go out there with the guys. Any time you get to play football live in a stadium, it’s a privilege,” he said. “Especially being able to go out there last week, you’re around it. Obviously I wasn’t playing, but you get that itch again.”
The Panthers will practice three more times before flying to Buffalo, giving Young three more chances to best the defense in the competitions that Canales stages during team periods. Young has been on the winning side in a lot of them, not that he’s spent much time rehashing them.
Nor was Young interested in discussing his strong camp and what it might mean for the season to come.
“I’m not a big sit back, reflect, compare (person). Doesn’t really do anything for me. So I don’t think about the past like that,” he said. “I’m happy with the camp we’re having so far. I’m happy with the growth as a unit. But it’s still early. We’ve got a lot more to do.”

full_text:
Safety Dillon Thieneman's speed has stood out so far in training camp for the Chicago Bears. Geoff Stellfox / Getty Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — Two weeks into Chicago Bears training camp, five of the team’s seven rookies have gotten a rep or two or many with the starters.
Whether it’s safety Dillon Thieneman, who’s started at safety from the beginning of camp, or sixth-round defensive tackle Jordan van den Berg, who rotates in for chances against the ones, several rookies are already showing progress.
Last year’s Bears featured four rookies as a major part of the offensive success — wide receiver Luther Burden, tight end Colston Loveland, offensive tackle Ozzy Trapilo and running back Kyle Monangai. Head coach Ben Johnson isn’t afraid to put a rookie on the field for big moments.
Here’s a look at the Bears’ 2026 draftees and how they’ve fared thus far.
Thieneman’s play speed is a major trait that drew the Bears to him in the back of Round 1. Part of the team’s offseason goal was getting faster on defense. Johnson has seen that translate on the field. Last week, someone mentioned to him that Thieneman’s practice “looked like his Oregon tape.”
“You can see that play speed start to show up,” Johnson said. “He is thinking a lot, and the way he’s wired is he wants to be on every little thing, so when you are like that, you can potentially, in your quest to be right every single time, slow down and … it’s just a matter of getting enough reps to where he can let loose and get after it. But really pleased with where he’s at.”
In Sunday’s practice, Thieneman appeared to have a minor injury and didn’t play every rep with the starting defense near the end of practice. One day prior, he showed his range to intercept a desperation heave from Caleb Williams. He also filled the run lane to stuff Kyle Monangai for a loss.
“Mentally, I think he’s going to be able to handle everything,” defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said last month. “So I think he’ll be a guy that I plan on picking things up pretty quickly.”
Jones has gotten zero reps with the starters. That’s Garrett Bradbury’s job. We haven’t seen much competition yet for Jones to earn some first-team reps or create any kind of rotation.
“Logan’s hungry, he’s got great football character, strong,” GM Ryan Poles said at the onset of camp. “From a physical standpoint, he’s in a really good place. But obviously as a young center, this game’s a lot different at this level. But we expect to get competition there as we go. Really happy with how Bradbury’s been.”
Jones has struggled in some one-on-one reps, but he’s also won a few battles, too, a reminder that we have to look at the whole picture. He showed some feistiness in team drills Sunday with a little post-play extracurricular with linebacker Ruben Hyppolite.
When the Bears are in “13 personnel,” Roush is the No. 3 tight end, as you’d expect from a third-rounder from Stanford with his pedigree.
“He’s a stud, he’s huge,” tight end Colston Loveland said. “First off. Big guy, super fast, strong. And just seeing him today with the pads on, he’s going to be a weapon for sure.”
Roush hasn’t necessarily done anything eye-popping as a pass catcher, but he’s made some nice plays. It’ll be important for him to keep getting the reps on special teams to be reliable for Richard Hightower’s units the way No. 3 tight end Durham Smythe was last season.
Thomas left Sunday’s session with an undisclosed injury. With Burden already sidelined, there’s an opportunity for Thomas to get more reps. We’ll hopefully learn in the coming days how minor or serious it is, as Thomas is the type of player who is going to keep growing with more receiver snaps. He has made some nice plays as a receiver.
As a returner, Thomas is getting lots of reps catching punts and kickoffs.
“I think that Zavion is a little bit more mature than most rookies that I’ve dealt with in the return position,” Hightower said Saturday. “… I think it’s a lot easier for him to adjust and adapt than most rookies I’ve had so far, so he’s been impressive, and he has tremendous speed.”
Injuries to Kyler Gordon and Jaylon Jones have opened the door for Muhammad to step in as the first-team nickel corner. With the second-team defense, he’ll play outside corner, a sign of his versatility and smarts, and the trust the coaching staff has in his ability to learn both.
In Saturday’s practice, Muhammad was noticeably active, notching a pass defensed early in practice.
“I see him going out and trying to execute the technique that we’re asking him to execute,” Allen said Sunday. “I see him playing with some confidence. I see him competing and being aggressive, and so those are all things that we want to see. He’s continued to get a little bit better every single day that he’s been out there, so that’s been good to see.”
Elliott remains on the PUP list with back discomfort and has yet to participate in training camp. He also missed minicamp and some of OTAs.
“He’s in really good shape. If you saw him walking around, you’d have no idea,” Poles said at the start of camp. “He’s running. Obviously, there is a return-to-play protocol where you are getting back to being a football player in terms of your strength, your conditioning, so he’ll be in that.”
It’s taking a while for Elliott to return, and he could’ve had some valuable reps, as T.J. Edwards missed the start of camp and D’Marco Jackson has been out the past two practices. He’ll have to get up to speed quickly, especially on special teams.
Based on draft position, van den Berg has been one of the bigger bright spots of camp, a sixth-rounder who consistently flashes his power and relentlessness. He’s a ball of energy at the snap and gives offensive linemen fits.
“He plays with great pad level, he can get in a good stance and come off and strike the line of scrimmage, and he’s got some pretty good football instincts and plays extremely hard,” Allen said. “A lot of the things that we saw on the tape at Georgia Tech, we’re seeing a lot of those same athletic qualities show up, and I think that’s what training camp is all about.”
Said veteran defensive tackle Neville Gallimore: “I think he’s gonna be a hell of a football player. I think he’s growing. His understanding of the game is improving every day. I just love his competitiveness. Great guy for the locker room.”
Van den Berg is still behind Grady Jarrett, Gervon Dexter, Gallimore and maybe Kentavius Street on the depth chart, but if he can be productive in the preseason games, too, he could earn a spot in the rotation for the start of the season.
• Safety Skyler Thomas has notable size (6 feet 2) in the back end and is getting a lot of reps considering all the injured veterans in front of him. When Thieneman had to sub out late in Sunday’s practice, Thomas was out there with the starters.
• Defensive tackle Jayden Loving is impressing his veteran teammates. “He’s super strong, super strong lower half, violent with his hands, great shoulder turn when he’s able to get going,” Jarrett said. “So I think he’s going to be somebody who’s definitely surprised a lot of people when these preseason games get going, and he’s going to represent for us really well.”
• Long snapper Beau Gardner won the competition, for now, when the Bears waived Luke Elkin to make room for another defensive back to help a depleted secondary. That’s a position where a team can always bring in a veteran if necessary, but it’s Gardner’s to keep at this point.

title: How Cowboys CB Shavon Revel has become one of the biggest camp standouts Two plays from practice Sunday while covering George Pickens paint a good picture of Revel's progression and mindset in Year 2. Jon Machota
summary:
After working his way back during his rookie season from a college knee injury, CB Shavon Revel looks more like the player the Cowboys expected when healthy. Kevin Jairaj / Imagn Images
OXNARD, Calif. — Shavon Revel was stunned. He dropped his head in disbelief. George Pickens had just done what he has been doing throughout the first two weeks of Dallas Cowboys training camp: making impressive catches.
But this one during red zone work on Saturday particularly bothered Revel because he was in gr
full_text:
After working his way back during his rookie season from a college knee injury, CB Shavon Revel looks more like the player the Cowboys expected when healthy. Kevin Jairaj / Imagn Images
OXNARD, Calif. — Shavon Revel was stunned. He dropped his head in disbelief. George Pickens had just done what he has been doing throughout the first two weeks of Dallas Cowboys training camp: making impressive catches.
But this one during red zone work on Saturday particularly bothered Revel because he was in great position to intercept the back-shoulder throw from Dak Prescott. Somehow, Pickens snatched the ball away at the last second.
Instead of allowing that to negatively impact the rest of practice, though, Revel came back about five minutes later and made a diving deflection on a throw intended for Pickens in the back of the end zone.
“I can’t believe he caught that,” Revel told The Athletic after Sunday’s practice. “Short memory. You gotta bounce back. There are great players like that. It’s gonna be 50-50 sometimes. At the end of the day, don’t give up on yourself. And that’s what I didn’t do.
“I just kept trying. They’re giving me the looks that I need, and sharpening my skills at the end of the day.”
Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer was not surprised by Revel’s response after the Pickens touchdown. Those are the expectations that have been set for the 2025 third-round pick who probably would have gone much earlier if not for a season-ending knee injury his final year of college.
Revel was still working his way back from the injury last season, wearing a protective brace in practice and games. No longer needing the brace, Revel is getting thrown in the fire, working with the first- and second-team defenses, covering all of Dallas’ top wide receivers, including stars Pickens and CeeDee Lamb.
“I think he’s responded that way the whole time,” Schottenheimer said of Revel’s impressive play on Saturday. “He’s going against a couple of the best in the league and he doesn’t back down at all. His confidence is growing. I watch him in meetings and he is literally hanging on every word that (defensive coordinator) Christian Parker, (defensive backs coach) Derrick Ansley and (secondary coach) Ryan Smith are saying.
“He’s very raw. Small-school guy, hasn’t played maybe a ton of football. But the talent is real. The makeup of the young man is real. And he is attacking his craft and really trying to learn the intricacies of playing corner in this system.”
Sunday’s practice was the most entertaining of camp, with highlight plays routinely being made on both sides of the ball. Revel was right in the mix. When it comes to listing early camp standouts, no one should be surprised when Pickens and Lamb are mentioned. But Revel is near the top of the list.
If the season started today, the two starting outside cornerbacks would probably be DaRon Bland and Cobie Durant. But Revel is knocking on the door.
“I feel great,” Revel said. “Way better than I did last year. Running-wise, cutting-wise, breaking-wise, it’s pretty sharp. You’re going to have bumps and bruises so I have to keep my treatment stuff together, and that’s what I’ve been doing.”
What is the next step for him?
“Just being consistent,” Revel said. “Situationally, third down, fourth down, what they might run in this formation. Those little things, I’m getting better at. It’s all coming together. There are little details that I want to fix in my game.”
Parker shared a similar response when asked about Revel. He wants to see the 25-year-old “making sure he’s able to live in a single play.”
“He has all the physical attributes,” Parker said. “Everything with him now is just working on everything from the neck up and just making sure that we’re thinking the game properly. And that’s a quick two- or three-second assessment because once you’re getting in your stance and you’re ready to play ball, you want to play with a clear mind.
“So just being able to do that and just finish plays. But he’s doing a good job. He’s extremely hardworking. He’s extremely willing. He wants to be coached. He runs towards that.”
Standing a legitimate 6-foot-2, 200 pounds, Revel excels in man coverage. The Cowboys are looking for him to improve in zone, something they believe has been progressing thanks to the extra time he’s been investing.
“He’s taken a big jump from last year,” Bland said. “He’s definitely honing in on his skills and techniques. Just keep learning. Every day he’s trying to learn.”
“He’s definitely super physical,” Pickens said. “I feel like him being that physical at the line of scrimmage can definitely deter a lot of other receivers in the league.”
Late in Sunday’s practice, veteran wide receiver Jonathan Mingo got past Revel on a deep ball up the left sideline. Revel caught up in time and knocked the pass away before Mingo got a chance to secure the grab.
“It felt great,” Revel said. “It was a little mental error. I picked it up real fast. Never gave up on the play, and that’s just kind of what was going through my head. I didn’t see the safety back there. So I was like, ‘Oh, damn, this is going to be my play.’ I just had to keep my head in the game, don’t panic. Just get out there and chase it. Don’t give up.”
It was a play that he likely would not have made a year ago. But now that he has the brace off and is moving like he did when he was a standout at East Carolina, Revel is looking like the player the Cowboys spoke so highly of following the draft.
And it’s easy to see his confidence has been elevated.
“Oh my gosh I can’t even tell you, but it’s like taking a deep breath,” he said. “It’s like you’ve been holding your breath under water forever and you can finally lift your head up out of the water and breathe that fresh air.”

title: Why won’t the Cowboys ever retire No. 88? It’s more than just a number Dan Pompei 1
summary:
Michael Irvin, center, and CeeDee Lamb, left, have carried on the Cowboys' No. 88 tradition, which began with Drew Pearson, right. Illustration: Kelsea Petersen / The Athletic; photos: Cooper Neill / Getty, Stephen Dunn / Getty
FRISCO, Texas — On the threshold of his seventh season, the latest No. 88 for the Dallas Cowboys soon will be competing with George Pickens for passes and with Quinyon Mitchell and Deonte Banks for space.
And then CeeDee Lamb will be competing with three long shadows for
full_text:
Michael Irvin, center, and CeeDee Lamb, left, have carried on the Cowboys' No. 88 tradition, which began with Drew Pearson, right. Illustration: Kelsea Petersen / The Athletic; photos: Cooper Neill / Getty, Stephen Dunn / Getty
FRISCO, Texas — On the threshold of his seventh season, the latest No. 88 for the Dallas Cowboys soon will be competing with George Pickens for passes and with Quinyon Mitchell and Deonte Banks for space.
And then CeeDee Lamb will be competing with three long shadows for his place in Cowboys lore.
The Cowboys’ 88 tradition is like no other, as the number has passed from Drew Pearson to Michael Irvin to Dez Bryant to Lamb, and between them, the 88s have 10 All-Pros, 16 Pro Bowls, four Super Bowl rings and two bronze busts.
Lamb is responsible for three of those All-Pros and five of those Pro Bowls but is coming off a season he was not pleased with, his least productive since his rookie year. So more than ever, he is determined to represent the number with dignity. He believes he will, partly because wisdom has been passed down along with his number.
“I feel smarter,” he says. “It’s just so close, and all it takes is a little more locking in.”
Lamb’s ambition is to be the best of the 88s. It is not an unreasonable aspiration.
“The 88 we got now is the most talented of us all,” Irvin says. “Drew was all about big plays. Small body, but he could get across that middle. I was just going to bully you. You know, not fast, none of that. Dez was a beast playing basketball outside. But CeeDee Lamb has all of it. He has all of it.”
Before the catch and after, Lamb combines finesse and power better than any of the 88s — or almost anyone else, for that matter. He creates separation like a good divorce lawyer, and his catch radius seems to range from the Fort Worth Stockyards to the Dallas Museum of Art.
Lamb probably would need a ring on one, two or three of his fingers to be crowned king of the 88s, but statistically, he is in their company. He needs just 44 yards to pass Bryant on the Cowboys’ all-time receiving list and 407 to pass Pearson. He trails Irvin by 4,488 yards, but if Lamb goes over 1,000 receiving yards this year for the sixth straight time, he will break a tie with Irvin for most consecutive 1,000-yard seasons.
Lamb says every time he opens his locker and sees 88, he thinks about the expectations — yours, his, theirs.
“When I have a big game, everybody celebrates,” he says. “When I have a bad game, there’s a lot of scrutiny, right? It’s a different magnitude when you’re in Dallas. And then it’s heightened when you wear 88.”
To understand why Irvin believes the number is “spiritual,” “divine” and “prophetic,” why it’s “the perfect looking number” and why, to him, it means “everything,” go back 53 years. As some NFL scouts wound their way from the University of Oklahoma to Oklahoma State, they stopped in Tulsa for a coffee or maybe something colder. While there, they checked out a defensive back and a defensive tackle but weren’t very interested in a wide receiver who had converted from quarterback as a junior. Pearson didn’t have the numbers, having caught 55 passes over two seasons and weighing 165 pounds. He ran for them anyway, registering a 4.6 in the 40-yard dash while wearing sweatpants so they couldn’t see his stork legs.
In January of 1973, 442 players were selected in the draft. Pearson was not among them. But he reported to the Cowboys that year with 82 other undrafted players and 17 draft picks. On a team that made it to the NFC Championship Game the year before and won the Super Bowl the year before that, Pearson wasn’t a long shot as much as a no-shot.
Between two-a-day practices in training camp that year, he worked a job with Merchant’s Van Lines for $10 an hour, loading trucks with refrigerators, televisions, furniture and caskets in heat that would make a mess of a chocolate bar.
For his first exhibition game against the Los Angeles Rams at the Los Angeles Coliseum, the jersey he found in his locker was No. 13, which nobody who was supposed to stick around would be wearing. But his feel between the line of scrimmage and the goal post was special, and he practiced with such gusto that he earned the favor of quarterback Roger Staubach. Somehow, Pearson made the team.
Wide receivers had to wear numbers in the 80s in those days, and the only available numbers were 85 and 88.
“Eighty-five didn’t sound right,” Pearson said. “What really sounded right was 88.”
Pearson was so thin that the first time he put his jersey on, the two eights overlapped, and it looked like his number was 8. He had to learn to tuck it in so both 8s showed. But he wore it well, starting six games as a rookie and becoming an All-Pro in his second season. With an abundance of instinct and a deficit of self-preservation, Pearson lasted 11 years and made so many game-changing catches that he became known as “Mr. Clutch.”
And that’s why No. 88 was Walter Irvin’s favorite player.
A Baptist preacher known as “Rev,” Walter was the father of 17 children, the 15th of whom was Michael. While Walter’s wife, Pearl, managed the kids, Walter fixed roofs with a pry bar and hammer during the week, then raised them with his sermons on the Lord’s Day.
Afterward, he always made time to watch America’s Team play America’s game. So devoted to the Cowboys was Rev that he wore his Tom Landry-style fedora to cheer for them in his living room. Young Michael had a seat next to Rev on their couch when Pearson caught the original “Hail Mary” from Staubach.
“He would always jump up when Drew scored a touchdown,” Michael says.
Predestiny? Michael’s sister Janet Carter is 10 years older than Michael. They always said she and Michael were Rev’s favorites. When Michael was 12, long before anyone else envisioned him as “The Playmaker,” Janet had a dream — she was walking through Texas Stadium with her little brother, who was a Dallas Cowboy.
As a senior at St. Thomas Aquinas High, Irvin played wide receiver for the first time and wore No. 80 because his favorite player was tight end Kellen Winslow, No. 80 for the San Diego Chargers. Winslow played with the same relentlessness as Irvin.
At the University of Miami, Irvin didn’t have a choice. They told Irvin he would wear 47. He protested to coach Jimmy Johnson, saying 47 was not a cool number.
“You know what I see when I see you wearing 47?” Johnson told him. “I see a 747 coming down the runway, ready to land for a touchdown.”
“Really, Coach?” the young Irvin said. “OK, I’ll take 47.”
The player and coach won a national championship at Miami and two Super Bowls together with the Cowboys, and then one day, Johnson, after a Heineken or three, told Irvin, “I can’t believe you bought that story about 47.”
Rev never saw any of it. He died before Michael’s senior year of high school. But Rev and Janet were in agreement about where Michael was headed.
Janet was so certain Michael would be a Cowboy that on draft day in ’88 — there’s that number again — she went shopping during the early selections, knowing she had time before the Cowboys picked 11th.
Michael, the final first-round pick of Landry’s career, was blown away when he was given his number, Pearson’s number.
“That was my dad,” Michael says. “You see what I’m saying? That was my dad.”
When Pearson heard the news, he was initially disappointed. No one had worn 88 since he retired, and he thought the number would be set aside like Staubach’s No. 12 had been. But then he thought about it.
What if Irvin and others could enhance the standard of excellence he established?
What if 88 became a legacy — his legacy?
When Irvin arrived in Dallas as a Cowboy for the first time, it was Pearson who greeted him at the airport. It was emotional, and they embraced. Ostensibly, Pearson was there to interview him for a local television station for which he was working. But really, he was there to pass the baton.
Irvin: “They want me to wear No. 88. Is that OK?”
Pearson: “I’m good with it.…

title: Vikings 53-man roster projection: Who is fighting for final spots during preseason? How is the Vikings roster shaping up after two weeks? There are several positions to watch aside from the competition at quarterback. Alec Lewis 1
summary:
Second-year receiver Tai Felton seems to have taken a significant step forward this summer and hopes to improve on his three receptions last season. David Berding / Getty Images
EAGAN, Minn. — The Minnesota Vikings’ annual training camp night practice usually marks a transition: The introductory phase is complete. The evaluation phase begins now.
All of the quarterback noise has overshadowed several other fascinating areas of the roster. Preseason games and joint practices with the Baltimore Rav
full_text:
Second-year receiver Tai Felton seems to have taken a significant step forward this summer and hopes to improve on his three receptions last season. David Berding / Getty Images
EAGAN, Minn. — The Minnesota Vikings’ annual training camp night practice usually marks a transition: The introductory phase is complete. The evaluation phase begins now.
All of the quarterback noise has overshadowed several other fascinating areas of the roster. Preseason games and joint practices with the Baltimore Ravens should tell us even more.
How are things shaping up after two weeks? Here is the first iteration of our roster projection:
In: Kyler Murray, J.J. McCarthy, Carson Wentz
The Vikings have given Murray the majority of the first-team reps in training camp. They believed this approach would build chemistry and help them evaluate his progress within the system. Murray’s performance has not been perfect by any stretch. On Sunday night, for example, he threw two interceptions in an 11-on-11 period and perhaps should’ve thrown another on a seven-on-seven rep.
McCarthy outperformed Murray on Sunday and on other days. But his consistency — and the efficiency of the offense — still appear to be a work in progress. Head coach Kevin O’Connell has not yet declared whether Murray or McCarthy will play in the preseason. The current challenge will be deciding on a starter in time for the first-team offense to get more reps and develop a rhythm, even though objective observers could be split on which quarterback has looked better.
In: Aaron Jones, Jordan Mason, Zavier Scott, Demond Claiborne
If you are searching for standouts at training camp, look for Mason. The 27-year-old returned this summer in exceptional shape, and his explosiveness shows up in team drills. O’Connell trusts Aaron Jones implicitly, but Mason’s burst and vision fit perfectly with the overhauled run concepts.
The depth conversation isn’t simple. Scott proved viable last preseason and became a trusted special teams option. His knowledge of O’Connell’s system helps his case. Meanwhile, Claiborne’s speed intrigued the Vikings enough to take a swing on him in the sixth round. His trajectory hinges on ball security and his ability to absorb the offense. Preseason games should offer him opportunities to generate confidence on both fronts.
Teams don’t draft fullbacks in the fifth round without a clear vision. Vikings assistant head coach Frank Smith knows what it looks like to creatively utilize the position to unlock angles in the run game. He saw Alec Ingold’s impact in Miami.
Bredeson, who, like Ingold, is a Wisconsin native, spent the first week of training camp lining up in all sorts of spots. His aptitude allows the coaches to add responsibilities to his plate.
In: Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, Jauan Jennings, Tai Felton, Myles Price
Out: Jeshaun Jones, Dontae Fleming, Dillon Bell, Michael Briscoe, Terrill Davis, Marcus Sanders Jr., Luke Wysong, Trayvon Rudolph
Praise is overdue for Felton, the team’s third-round pick in 2025. The Maryland product made a one-handed catch last week that created buzz. The highlight captured Felton’s continuing progression, which has been evident almost daily. He releases from the line of scrimmage with a plan. He runs routes with improved smoothness. Last year, he dropped a noticeable number of passes. The reliability of his hands remains something to monitor.
It will be interesting to see how the Vikings round out the room behind Felton and Price. Fleming, who played at Tulane before signing as an undrafted free agent last spring, is a critical name to keep tabs on throughout the preseason.
In: T.J. Hockenson, Josh Oliver, Gavin Bartholomew
Out: Ben Yurosek, Bryson Nesbit
This position feels a bit overlooked. Hockenson has had a quiet camp, and Oliver’s role tends to keep him under the radar. That said, both players need to stay healthy to allow the Vikings offense to dictate personnel matchups to defenses the way they envisioned.
Hockenson and Oliver have missed games due to injuries in recent years, which places more emphasis on their backups. Last year, Yurosek performed admirably. Bartholomew’s pass-catching talent may give him more upside, but even if he establishes himself as worthy of the No. 3 role, the Vikings will be betting big on alternatives in the event of an injury.
In: LT Christian Darrisaw, LG Donovan Jackson, C Blake Brandel, RG Will Fries, RT Brian O’Neill, T Ryan Van Demark, G Joe Huber, T Caleb Tiernan, C Michael Jurgens
Out: Henry Byrd, Gavin Gerhardt, Walter Rouse, Caleb Etienne, Vershon Lee, Tomas Rimac, Delby Lemieux, Tristan Leigh
The biggest question mark here — and one of the most important subjects when it comes to the 2026 team — is Brandel. The 29-year-old had never played center before Week 5 of last season. Interior pressure affects all quarterbacks, but Murray’s smaller stature makes him even more susceptible. This will shine an even brighter spotlight on Brandel.
Behind the starters, Van Demark and Tiernan are shoo-ins. Jurgens currently edges Gerhardt at the backup center spot. Huber and Byrd may spend the majority of the preseason in the thick of a competition to back up at guard.
In: Jalen Redmond, Levi Drake Rodriguez, Caleb Banks, Domonique Orange, Isaiahh Loudermilk
Out: Elijah Williams, Eric Johnson II, Taki Taimani, Smith Vilbert, Monkell Goodwine
Defensive coordinator Brian Flores’ non-traditional system makes projections like these tedious. Redmond, Rodriguez, Banks and Orange are guaranteed to make the roster. The rest of this room requires further evaluation.
Loudermilk, who played for the Steelers from 2021 to 2025, has taken snaps with the second-team defense. On the other hand, Williams, an undrafted free agent from Morgan State, had such a successful 2025 camp that the Vikings kept him. Minnesota could keep six here, though that would complicate numbers elsewhere.
In: Andrew Van Ginkel, Dallas Turner, Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins, Bo Richter and Chaz Chambliss
Out: Tyler Batty, Cam’Ron Stewart, Arden Walker
Ingram-Dawkins returned to Minnesota for his second season in exceptional shape. The 6-foot-5, 290-pounder gives the defensive staff another movable body up front. Like Banks, he can play an assortment of positions. Richter, Chambliss and Batty bring special teams experience and production.
However, the Vikings still don’t have an obvious replacement for Turner at pass-rush end in the event of an injury. They still possess cap space. Multiple free-agent edge rushers are available, so another signing is firmly in play.
In: Blake Cashman, Eric Wilson, Jake Golday, Ivan Pace Jr., Jamal Adams
Out: Josh Ross, Keli Lawson, Bangally Kamara, Jacob Roberts
Many of these linebackers play multiple spots. Wilson can rush the passer from the edge. Golday has already mixed in at Andrew Van Ginkel’s edge position. Adams has already switched numbers, allowing him to line up at slot defender or safety.
The more hybrid personnel offenses use, the more defenses will need tweener bodies to match. You can see the vision with the players the Vikings have added. If offenses want to use big-bodied sets to throw more often, the Vikings have the mobile defenders to counteract it.
In: Byron Murphy Jr., Isaiah Rodgers, James Pierre, Charles Demmings
Out: Zemaiah Vaughn, Dwight McGlothern, Da’Veawn Armstead, Marcus Allen, Tyreek Chappell, Jarod Washington
Four cornerbacks may feel thin, but the Vikings frequently use safeties as slot defenders, which lessens the need for several backup options. Keeping only four corners also makes sense, as the gaps between many of the former undrafted cornerbacks aren’t large.
Murphy looks motivated and has since the spring. Rodgers is entering a contract season, and Pierre has a chance to further establish himself as a worthy starter. If any of these three suffer injuries, Minnesota can turn to perhaps its most promising young cornerback in years. In training camp, few defenders have made more plays on the ball…

title: Patriots training camp: Risers and fallers as first preseason game looms Christian Gonzalez, Will Campbell and this unproven receiver have been among the Patriots players to impress so far in training camp. Chad Graff
summary:
Receiver DeMario Douglas has looked great in training camp before but has never broken out in the regular season. Eric Canha / Imagn Images
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — After five straight practices that concluded with an intrasquad scrimmage Friday, the New England Patriots were off over the weekend.
They return this week with a busy schedule on tap. Their first of three joint practices (this one with the Indianapolis Colts) is Tuesday. Their first preseason game is Thursday.
So to reset before an event
full_text:
Receiver DeMario Douglas has looked great in training camp before but has never broken out in the regular season. Eric Canha / Imagn Images
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — After five straight practices that concluded with an intrasquad scrimmage Friday, the New England Patriots were off over the weekend.
They return this week with a busy schedule on tap. Their first of three joint practices (this one with the Indianapolis Colts) is Tuesday. Their first preseason game is Thursday.
So to reset before an eventful few days, let’s look at the Patriots who are rising or falling after two weeks of training camp.
I hesitated with this one. You could argue that Douglas has been a riser in every training camp, but his strong July and August starts haven’t translated to the massive breakout many have predicted. So it’s valid to be in wait-and-see mode with Douglas.
Still, I put him here for two reasons. First, he just keeps making plays, including a deep ball in Friday’s scrimmage and a grab in the end zone. The second is that the Patriots seem more willing to feature him in the offense, often using him as the third receiver in 11 personnel.
I get it if you’re skeptical, given how often we’ve seen Douglas featured in categories like this one. But I’m buying the hype again.
The Patriots could still look to the waiver wire in a couple of weeks for tight end help, but for now it seems pretty clear which tight end they trust most for the blocking role left vacant by Julian Hill’s season-ending injury.
Arkin’s upside in the passing game is limited, but it seems the Patriots want a No. 3 tight end both to play in 13 personnel (which the Los Angeles Rams used so well a year ago) and as a blocking option in short-yardage situations. At 262 pounds, Arkin is a big tight end, but that size shows up in his blocking prowess.
With the Patriots struggling to find linebacker depth a year ago, they signed Muma off the Indianapolis Colts’ practice squad last December. At the time, it seemed like a short-term fix.
But Muma is now practicing with the Patriots’ starting base defense alongside Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss.
Muma brings an athletic profile to the position that Spillane and Elliss lack, with the speed (4.63-second 40) and explosiveness (a 40-inch vertical leap) to run with tight ends.
It’s well documented that Campbell’s playoff performance didn’t go as planned after he suffered a late-season knee injury.
But Campbell has shown up to training camp looking exactly the way you’d want a second-year former first-round pick to look. He has missed the last two practices while sporting an elbow brace, but it doesn’t look too serious considering coach Mike Vrabel said he expects the 22-year-old to practice this week.
More importantly, Campbell has done an impressive job against the New England edge rushers in camp. Maybe that speaks to the players they currently have on the edge, but it’s notable nonetheless.
With Carlton Davis missing several practices, the Patriots have used a few different players opposite Christian Gonzalez on the outside. But Prunty is the one who most looks the part.
The fifth-round rookie has good size for the outside (6-foot-1 with nearly 32-inch arms) and great speed (4.45-second 40) and has impressed in camp with better-than-expected ball skills after nabbing just two interceptions over his last three collegiate seasons.
OK, maybe this is unfair. How can Gonzalez be considered a “riser” when he is already seen as one of the best in the NFL at his position?
But the 24-year-old has risen to the challenge of continually going up against a big, physical No. 1 wide receiver in A.J. Brown and often gets the better of him. He’s in the midst of a lengthy contract negotiation, but it doesn’t seem to have impacted his play. He looks primed for a monster season.
This one feels a little conflicted.
On the one hand, everything Vrabel has said suggests that Williams’ spot on the roster is safe and that the team plans to carve out a role for him. Vrabel even named Williams an offseason award winner.
On the other hand, Williams spends most practices with the second-team offense and doesn’t often stand out, even against the backups.
The open kick-return job will probably be an important one in determining how much Williams sees the field this season.
After Hill’s injury, the door was wide open for backup tight ends to make an impression. But Dippre was limited by an injury and only recently rejoined practices.
In the meantime, rookie Eli Raridon has impressed in the passing game, and Arkin has impressed in the run game.
That leaves Dippre behind the eight ball with three weeks remaining until roster cutdown day.
Similar to tight end, the No. 3 running back job was wide open. It still is.
Larison seemed to get the first chance at the gig early in training camp, but it seems he didn’t do enough to secure the job. With preseason games approaching, the guess here is that Terrell Jennings and Jam Miller are a bit ahead of Larison on the depth chart.
The Patriots’ backup interior linemen have been so mediocre that the team brought in veterans for tryouts. Coaches even flipped James Hudson and rookie Caleb Lomu to guard for stretches.
It was always a bit surprising that the Patriots didn’t do more this offseason to bolster their interior depth, especially given Alijah Vera-Tucker’s injury history and Jared Wilson’s struggles as a rookie.
Look, it can be difficult to rate cornerback play in 11-on-11 practices. You don’t know what the defensive play call was or if a big gain happened because of a mistake from someone else.
That said, receivers have made too many plays in front of Minor to ignore, and the second-year man looks like he’s behind Gonzalez, Davis, Prunty, Charles Woods, Kindle Vildor and Channing Canada on the depth chart.

full_text:
Philadelphia Eagles rookie WR Makai Lemon has dealt with hamstring injuries during training camp so far. Mitchell Leff / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — The preseason has arrived. The Philadelphia Eagles had a scheduled off day on Sunday. They are returning to practice Monday for the first of three full practices, plus two walk-throughs, leading up to Saturday’s preseason opener against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium.
Sunday’s off day followed the team’s longest uninterrupted stretch of training camp: five practices and a walk-through over six days. There is much to review. The Athletic ’s Zach Berman and Brooks Kubena analyzed the second week of training camp and what’s ahead this week.
Kubena: The defense’s depth. Entering training camp, I had one question regarding the overall strength of its starters: edge rusher. The strength of the defense’s depth stood out to me this past week — particularly at safety and linebacker, both of which have dealt with long-term injuries in recent seasons.
The Eagles seem to have two solid options at safety between Marcus Epps and Michael Carter II. If Epps wins that position battle, Carter is still proving he can make plays as a safety, nickel and the secondary’s dime defender. Carter tracked a Jalen Hurts deep ball in coverage against Hollywood Brown and snagged an interception in Wednesday’s practice.
Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio is pleased with his progression. Jeremiah Trotter Jr. is also catching my attention frequently at linebacker. He’s filling running lanes quickly, blitzing effectively and punching out passes in coverage. Jihaad Campbell has been less consistent in coverage, and Trotter’s availability makes that less of a concern to me.
Berman: I’ll go over to offense. With DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon’s injuries, we’ve had more exposure to the rest of the receiver depth chart. I’ve been impressed by the depth, which is better than it has been in previous years. Dontayvion Wicks stood out, earned the trust of Jalen Hurts and is demonstrating why he’s a top three receiver on this team. (And he might be closer to No. 2 than No. 3 entering the season.)
If you did not know Darius Cooper’s background and simply observed practices, you’d think he’s a surefire player on the 53-man roster. Hollywood Brown and Elijah Moore both made plays with the first-team offense. Johnny Wilson came alive on Friday with a few nice catches. I’m still concerned about the wide receiver group because the top of the depth chart is a drop-off from the previous four seasons. Even if Smith can replace A.J. Brown’s production, it’s going to be hard to replace Smith’s presence as the No. 2. But I think Nos. 3-6 are in better shape than the past. That would support the idea of collectively replacing his production.
Kubena: Lane Johnson’s announcement on Saturday obviously warrants this discussion. His words carry significant weight, and he called Markel Bell “one of the best rookies I’ve been around.” That endorsement is enough for me to feel confident about the franchise’s future at right tackle.
We got a chance to see Bell play right tackle for the first time during Johnson’s four-practice absence, and, to borrow Bell’s words, he did experience some “growing pains.” Johnson had told him he would. But when I see Bell absorb Jalyx Hunt’s power rushes and keep pace with Nolan Smith’s speed rushes, I think I see part of what Johnson sees.
It is lofty to place All-Pro expectations on Bell as Johnson’s successor. The lineage of tackles dating back to Jason Peters makes that difficult to avoid. And, given Johnson’s status as a former first-round pick, and Peters’ arrival partly at the cost of a 2009 first-rounder, there is a tendency to think the Eagles ought to spend an equivalent investment on Johnson’s successor. But the Eagles have enjoyed elite play from former seventh-rounder Jordan Mailata, even though they had two full seasons to develop him in the background. Bell must soak up all he can this year from Johnson — and it still may take a few years for him to reach the position group’s standard.
As for the interior, I am less convinced of their current and future depth there than new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion was Saturday, when he included Drew Kendall in his overall statement that the O-line has “a really good crop of young players as well.” It is not an encouraging sight to see center Cam Jurgens twice leave practice early and left guard Landon Dickerson sub out in first-team drills — even if it is part of a load management plan. (It is a reminder that both players require one.) Another draft cycle with greater investment in the interior would serve the Eagles well.
Berman: If the starters are healthy, I’m comfortable with this group. That seems to be an annual statement from me, though. We’ll see if there’s anything to Jurgens exiting early the past two sessions. I like how Kendall played and believe they can get by with him if they need a reserve for a week or two. I’d be less enthusiastic about that option for a season-long replacement. And if there are two injuries on the interior, it’s even more concerning. At tackle, Bell has seemed to usurp Fred Johnson as the swing tackle. I don’t know if that’s as much due to the way Bell’s playing or Fred Johnson’s playing, but I’d agree I’ve seen some good signs from Bell.
Still, I’m not yet convinced that Bell is Lane Johnson’s heir apparent. I wouldn’t rule it out, but for an organization keen on succession plans, I’m not sure they’d see a high third-round pick as the surefire replacement. (You’re correct about Mailata, although that wasn’t the plan. The Eagles drafted Andre Dillard in the first round to become a starting tackle.) If Bell can develop this year — and the tools are present — it would be an ideal outcome for the franchise as it would not need to push tackle in the draft. I’ve predicted the Eagles would take an offensive tackle in the first round in two of the last three mock drafts. I was wrong, although my guess is Howie Roseman would have been surprised had you told him three years ago that he’d go through the next three first and second rounds without addressing the position. So I’d say to readers: Hope Bell blossoms, but don’t disregard Dane Brugler’s offensive tackle rankings.
Kubena: I am less concerned about DeVonta Smith’s pathway back to the field. He missed two November games with a hamstring injury in 2024 and closed that regular season with two 100-yard games. He also managed a hamstring injury before Super Bowl LIX and still delivered his dagger of a 46-yard touchdown catch in that game. Makai Lemon still has much to learn in this offense. Recall how Cooper DeJean suffered a hamstring injury before training camp during his rookie season, returned to joint practices with the New England Patriots, and still did not start at nickel until Week 5. One could argue DeJean had more to learn in moving to a completely new position. But Mannion’s system is much different than the shotgun-spread system Lemon thrived in at USC. On-field reps are invaluable to his development, and projections of him being a Week 1 contributor go down the longer he’s out. Elijah Moore had a good week of practice. It does, for now, look like the Eagles don’t have to be nudged to dump more on Lemon’s plate than is required.
Berman: There haven’t been any season-ending injuries, which is a good sign. I’ve seen those pop up in other camps, and Washington just lost Laremy Tunsil for an extended period. The goal is to get to Week 1 healthy. At wide receiver, I don’t think a hamstring injury is ever something to dismiss. You don’t know if it’s an injury that can linger or must be managed during the season. (Also: Remember when injuries to the offensive linemen and Jalen Carter were not a major concern to the team last summer? You don’t want lingering injuries affecting a front-line player during the season.)
I feel the same way you do about both DeVonta Smith and Lemon. With…

full_text:
De'Zhaun Stribling has impressed 49ers coaches, but has really caught the attention of the team's defensive backs in training camp. Sergio Estrada / Imagn Images
SANTA CLARA, Calif. — Mac Jones wants to call him “The Flyin’ Hawaiian.”
And while 49ers rookie De’Zhaun Stribling, who hails from Honolulu, has shown off his speed in training camp, the team’s cornerbacks are more impressed with another facet of his game.
“I ain’t gonna lie — No. 1 is his hands,” said cornerback Deommodore Lenoir.
Said nickelback Upton Stout: “I like the way he uses his hands and his speed. He’s gonna be a good addition for us.”
The rookie’s hands measure 10 inches, a big number for a receiver. To put that in perspective, they’re the same size as 6-foot-6, 332-pound defensive tackle Alfred Collins’ mitts.
And Stribling’s been using them in different ways: at the beginning of his route to get past cornerbacks playing press coverage; at the top of the route to create separation; and, most notably, to catch passes in traffic.
“I would say him just catching away from his body, just kind of trusting his hands,” Lenoir said of Stribling’s strength. “He’s got that catch radius where he’s gonna catch it away from his body. He’s got strong fingertips.”
Apart from missing three days of practice with hamstring tightness, everything appears to be going according to plan so far with Stribling, a surprise — and highly critiqued — selection at pick No. 33 in April.
Wide receivers coach Leonard Hankerson said Sunday the rookie has mostly worked at the F and X positions in training camp. That suggests he’ll help fill the role Jauan Jennings (F) had in recent seasons while also stepping in at times for Mike Evans (X). He hasn’t played as much Z, the position the team was hoping Ricky Pearsall, out for the season with a lingering PCL injury, would play in 2026. Instead, it looks like that spot will go to Deebo Samuel and others.
“No one here is wired exactly how Ricky is,” Kyle Shanahan said Saturday. “They’re all a little bit different. So you do lose a big part of what we were planning on. That’s where guys do have to step up. That’s what gets frustrating when guys like Stribling tweak a muscle and stuff, because, yeah you want guys to step up, but you’ve got to train them to do it. They’ve got to work to do it. They’ve got to be out there to be able to do it at an NFL level, which is coming real fast.”
Stribling seems like a particularly good replacement for Jennings, who’s now with the Minnesota Vikings. For one, he was a strong blocker in college, something that became Jennings’ calling card during his six years in San Francisco.
He’s also looked efficient on contested catches in the middle of the field, which was another Jennings’ forte.
“It’s not just that he’s catching it,” Hankerson said. “He’s strong. He’s attacking it. He’s stepping back to (the ball). With the contested catch situation, he’s able to come down with a lot of those. Right now, I can’t really recall him putting one on the ground.”
Lining up at the F or slot position has created regular matchups with Stout, who’s also having a strong camp. He and the other cornerbacks have more license to play aggressively this year, which suits their styles and has led to plenty of tipped passes and incompletions in the middle of the field. That close coverage has vexed receivers like Jacob Cowing and Jordan Watkins, with Watkins in particular having an issue with contested catches early in training camp.
But Stribling has looked confident with a cornerback or safety draped over his back.
“He’s going to be a dog,” Stout said.
Where Stribling could separate himself from Jennings is, well, separation. While Jennings clocked a 4.72-second 40 before the 2020 draft, Stribling’s this year was 4.36 seconds. The 49ers hope that translates into a lot of yards after the catch and the occasional deep ball when defensive backs creep up to clog the middle.
“I call him the Flyin’ Hawaiian because he’s so fast,” Jones said. “… He has, like, a second gear when the ball’s in the air. Some guys are really fast, but when the ball goes up and your eyes go up, you slow down. But he doesn’t do that, so it’s pretty impressive.”
